title: Attention Please! - Why Attention is the Gateway to Learning
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Clark opens his DistillED newsletter by presenting Daniel Willingham's Simple Model of the Mind (attention, working memory, long-term memory) as the shared framework for his school's staff workshops. His central claim is that attention is the gateway to learning, because students learn what they think about and working memory is too limited to cope with divided focus. He treats distraction from displays, cluttered slides and chatter as competition for scarce mental bandwidth. The piece then moves from cognitive science to practice with five classroom moves for securing attention. These are a Do Now, fewer distractions, attentional cues, accountable questioning and visuals that direct focus. It closes with pointers to further resources on attention and classroom management.
points: Attention is framed as the gateway to learning: students remember what they think about, whether or not it is the intended learning.
Working-memory limits mean divided attention leaves too little capacity to process new material, so lessons must be designed to provoke hard thinking.
Environmental fixes such as simpler slides and strategic seating are presented as cheap ways to free up attention.
Routines like a retrieval-based Do Now and a call-and-response attention cue build attentional habits.
Cold calling and turn-and-talk keep every student cognitively accountable for a possible response.
quotes: Attention is important because it is the gateway to learning. To secure students’ attention is not easy—students don’t always focus on what we want them to. This can be down to distractions in the environment—from classroom displays, poorly designed slides to off-task chatter—compete for mental bandwidth.

Educational psychologist Daniel Willingham explains that students actively learn what they think about. In other words, if students are thinking about what’s for lunch or how to sharpen a pencil or how pretty your PowerPoint images are, that’s what will be remembered—not the learning intention. Educators must carefully design lessons that promote hard thinking.

Research from cognitive science tells us that working memory is limited—we can only juggle a few pieces of information at once (Sweller et al., 2019). If students’ attention is divided or directed at the wrong things, they simply don’t have the cognitive capacity to process new information effectively.
Without attention, even the best-planned lesson falls flat. So, how can we manage the environment and actively secure attention to ensure that learning occurs?

Begin lessons with a short, focused task that activates prior knowledge and sets the tone. Make it routine, visible, and independent. For example, a short retrieval quiz or question as students enter.
Simplify your slide decks. Reduce the clutter. Seat students strategically to avoid distractions. Small tweaks to the environment free up attention.
Keep students cognitively on the hook. Cold call or use “turn and talk,” to ensure all students know they may be invited to share.
